slides.note: Making EPO, active vitamin D and renin are the kidney's endocrine jobs, each done by a different cell. EPO (erythropoietin) comes from fibroblast-like interstitial cells of the cortex when O₂ stays low. PCT (proximal convoluted tubule) cells make the final, active vitamin D (calcitriol). Renin comes from the JG cells (juxtaglomerular cells) of the afferent arteriole. The nephrons and collecting ducts are the exocrine part: their product is urine. Gluconeogenesis (in PCT cells) is a metabolic job, not an endocrine one.

Black arrows show which way the fluid flows. Follow the tube from the corpuscle: PCT (light green) → proximal straight tubule (lilac) → thin descending limb → thin ascending limb → thick ascending limb (yellow) → macula densa (purple patch that touches its own corpuscle) → DCT (distal convoluted tubule, dark green) → connecting tubule (orange) → collecting duct. Corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie only in the cortex; the loops and collecting ducts run down into the medulla.

The connecting tubules of several nephrons empty into one collecting duct. Ducts merge as they descend and open at the tip of the papilla as the papillary ducts of Bellini. In this older drawing, 'thick descending limb' means the proximal straight tubule.

Cortical nephrons (most nephrons) sit high in the cortex and have short loops that barely enter the medulla. Juxtamedullary nephrons (about 1 in 7) sit next to the medulla and have long loops that reach deep toward the papilla. These long loops build the very salty (hypertonic) inner medulla that lets the kidney make concentrated urine.

Blood passes two capillary beds in a row, joined by the efferent arteriole. Draining the glomerulus by an arteriole, not a venule, keeps glomerular pressure high. Follow the middle boxes down: interlobular artery → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole; each box's line points to that vessel in the nephron drawing (right). Efferent arterioles of cortical nephrons form peritubular capillaries; water and solutes that the tubules reabsorb pass into them and return to the blood. Those of juxtamedullary nephrons form the vasa recta: long hairpin capillaries beside the loops of Henle.

Each corpuscle has two poles. At the vascular pole the afferent arteriole enters and the efferent arteriole leaves. At the tubular pole the capsular (urinary) space drains into the PCT. The parietal layer (outer wall) is simple squamous epithelium that turns into the cuboidal PCT epithelium at the tubular pole. The visceral layer is the podocytes hugging the capillaries.

Each layer stops something different. Endothelial fenestrations (pores) stop blood cells and platelets. The GBM (glomerular basement membrane) stops large proteins. The slit diaphragms between podocyte feet stop many small proteins.

The GBM is unusually thick (about 300 nm) because two basal laminae, one from the endothelium and one from the podocytes, fuse into one. Type IV collagen forms a mesh that blocks large proteins. Heparan sulfate proteoglycans give it a negative charge that repels negatively charged proteins such as albumin.
SEM (scanning electron microscopy) shows surfaces in 3-D. P = podocyte cell bodies. C = capillaries, covered by the fine, interlocking pedicels (the comb-like texture).

Nephrin molecules from facing pedicels (podocyte foot processes) meet in the middle of the slit like a zipper. Podocin and CD2AP anchor nephrin to the pedicel's actin. Without working nephrin (congenital nephrotic syndrome), the slit diaphragm fails and protein leaks into the urine.

Answer: the 3 layers (right image, left to right: from the capillary lumen C toward the urinary space): (1) endothelium (E) with pores (F, fenestrations); (2) the thick basement membrane (BM); (3) pedicels (P) separated by filtration slits (FS), each bridged by a thin slit diaphragm (SD). Left image: C = capillary lumen with red blood cells, PC = podocyte cell bodies, CS = capsular space. The box is enlarged on the right.

Albumin (about 67 kDa, kilodaltons) sits right at the size cut-off. What keeps it out is mainly charge: albumin is negative, and so is the barrier. So normal urine has almost no albumin. When the barrier is damaged (diabetes, glomerulonephritis), protein leaks out: proteinuria.

Mesangial cells sit in the stalk between capillary loops, on the capillary surfaces that podocytes don't cover. Like pericytes, they are contractile cells that hug capillaries. Left: the dark brown star with a blue nucleus is the mesangial cell; the tan material around it is the mesangial matrix. Right: the mesangium is the darker-stained cells and matrix in the center, between the capillary lumens (white spaces; the solid dark-blue shapes in them are red blood cells).

MC = mesangial cell; MM = mesangial matrix, which merges with the basement membrane (BM) where podocytes are absent. Arrows = contractile mesangial processes along the capillaries. E = red blood cell, L = lymphocyte, EC = endothelial cell, P = podocyte, PD = pedicels, US = urinary space, asterisks = capillary lumen.

Left (H&E, low power): the dark pink cortex on top holds the round corpuscles; the paler, striped medulla narrows to the papilla below. Pale stripes running up into the cortex are medullary rays. Its pointer lines carry no labels; the red-filled tubes are blood vessels. Right key: 1 corpuscle, 2 PCT, 3 proximal straight tubule, 4 thin descending limb, 5 thin ascending limb, 6 thick ascending limb, 7 macula densa, 8 DCT, 9 connecting tubule (9* an arching one), 10 cortical collecting duct (in the shaded medullary ray), 11 outer and 12 inner medullary collecting duct.

Answer (tell them apart by position). Podocytes: nuclei on the outer surface of capillary loops, bulging into the white urinary space. Endothelial cells: small flat nuclei lining the capillary lumens. Mesangial cells: darker nuclei in the stalks where loops meet. Parietal cells: flat nuclei lining the outer wall of Bowman's capsule. H&E = hematoxylin and eosin (nuclei purple, cytoplasm pink).

RC = renal corpuscles. CL = cortical labyrinth: corpuscles plus twisted (convoluted) tubules cut in all directions. MR = medullary rays: bands of straight tubules running in parallel (proximal straight tubules, thick ascending limbs, collecting ducts). Quick rule: a medullary ray has no corpuscles.

PCT vs DCT. PCT: big cells with deep pink (eosinophilic) cytoplasm from many mitochondria, only 3–5 nuclei per cross-section, blurry cell borders, and a fuzzy, 'filled' lumen from the brush border (long microvilli). DCT: smaller, paler cells, more nuclei crowded together, and a clean, open lumen with no brush border. PCTs far outnumber DCTs because the PCT is much longer. Right: the big fuzzy tubules are PCTs; the small ones with crowded nuclei (top center, top right corner, lower right) are DCTs.

TEM (transmission electron microscopy) of a PCT cell; the lumen is at the top. MV = tall microvilli (brush border), a huge surface for reabsorption. V = vesicles taking up filtered small proteins, which L = lysosomes digest to amino acids. M = long mitochondria packed in the basal membrane folds; they power the Na⁺ pumps. Reabsorbed water and solutes leave the base of the cell and enter the capillary (C) at the bottom. F = fibroblast process.

JGA (juxtaglomerular apparatus) = where the distal tubule touches its own corpuscle's arterioles, at the vascular pole. Arrows: black = blood flow, green = filtrate flow. Macula densa: tall, crowded cells at the end of the thick ascending limb, where it becomes the DCT (labeled 'distal tubule' here); they sense NaCl in the tubular fluid. High NaCl makes the afferent arteriole constrict, lowering GFR (glomerular filtration rate). JG cells: modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin. Lacis cells (extraglomerular mesangial cells) sit between the two arterioles; they are not labeled here.

Left (trichrome stain): MD = macula densa, the row of tall cells with crowded nuclei in the wall of the distal tubule (D). JG = juxtaglomerular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole (AA). L = lacis (extraglomerular mesangial) cells. EA = efferent arteriole, G = glomerulus, US = urinary space, P = proximal tubules with filled lumens.

Low blood pressure makes the JG cells release renin. Renin cuts angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I. ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) in lung capillaries turns it into angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles and makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting ducts reabsorb more Na⁺ (move it out of the tubule fluid back into the blood); water follows, so blood volume and pressure rise.

Medulla cut across: no corpuscles, no convoluted tubules. Collecting ducts: the largest tubules (e.g. center), with pale cuboidal-to-columnar cells, sharp cell borders and round central nuclei. Thick ascending limbs: the smaller rings of deep-pink cuboidal cells, no brush border. Thin limbs: tiny tubes of flat (squamous) cells in between. Don't confuse a thin limb with a vasa recta capillary: the capillary usually holds red blood cells and has a thinner wall.

ADH (antidiuretic hormone, vasopressin) comes from the posterior pituitary. It binds the collecting-duct principal cells and moves stored aquaporin (water-channel) vesicles into the luminal membrane. Water then moves out of the duct (arrows) into the salty medulla and is carried away by the vasa recta: a small volume of concentrated urine. The late distal tubule (top arrow) responds the same way. Without ADH the duct stays water-tight: a large volume of dilute urine. Micrograph: CD = collecting duct (pale cells, distinct borders); VR = vasa recta.

Transitional epithelium (urothelium) is stratified, but its surface cells are large, dome-shaped umbrella cells (sometimes with two nuclei). In stratified squamous epithelium the surface cells are flat. Urothelium stretches: 5–7 cell layers when the bladder is empty, 2–3 when full. It also lines the first part of the urethra.

Recognize the ureter: a small tube with a star-shaped lumen (longitudinal mucosal folds), lined by transitional epithelium. Its smooth-muscle layer (Mu) is much thicker than the mucosa (M). Outside is adventitia (A). The muscle moves urine to the bladder by peristalsis.

(a) Bladder wall: U = urothelium, LP = lamina propria, S = submucosa, then three smooth-muscle layers IL, ML, OL (inner, middle, outer; together the detrusor muscle), A = adventitia. (b) Empty bladder: mucosa deeply folded, urothelium thick, umbrella cells bulging (collagen stained red). (c) Full bladder: mucosa smooth, urothelium thin, umbrella cells flattened.

Urethra (b enlarges the box in a): the mucosa has large longitudinal folds around the lumen (L). Its lining (E) is mostly stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium. It starts as transitional epithelium next to the bladder and ends as stratified squamous epithelium at the outside opening.

qs.q: Which kidney cells secrete renin?
opts: Fibroblast-like interstitial cells of the cortex
Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole
Macula densa cells of the distal tubule
qs.why: JG cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole wall that store and release renin.

qs.q: Which kidney cells release erythropoietin when O₂ stays low?
opts: Principal cells of the collecting duct
Juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
Fibroblast-like interstitial cells of the cortex
qs.why: Erythropoietin comes from fibroblast-like interstitial cells in the cortex; it drives red cell production in the bone marrow.

qs.q: Which kidney cells make the active form of vitamin D (calcitriol)?
qs.why: PCT cells add the final hydroxyl group that turns vitamin D into calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D₃).

qs.q: Which structures form the kidney's exocrine part?
qs.why: Nephrons and collecting ducts make urine, an external product; renin, erythropoietin and calcitriol are the endocrine outputs.

qs.q: A uriniferous tubule is made of which two embryologically distinct parts?
opts: Loop of Henle and connecting tubule
qs.why: The nephron makes urine and the collecting duct finishes concentrating it; the two come from different embryonic tissues.

qs.q: Where are renal corpuscles always found?
qs.why: Corpuscles and convoluted tubules lie only in the cortex; loops of Henle and collecting ducts run down into the medulla.

qs.q: Collecting ducts open at the tip of the papilla as which ducts?
qs.why: Collecting ducts merge as they descend and empty into the minor calyx as papillary ducts of Bellini.

qs.q: What do the long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons make possible?
opts: A hypertonic inner medulla for concentrating urine
Filtering more plasma than cortical nephrons
qs.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons (about 1 in 7) have long loops reaching toward the papilla that build the salty inner medulla; cortical nephrons have short loops.

qs.q: Afferent arterioles branch directly from which arteries?
qs.why: The route is renal → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arteriole.

qs.q: Why does an efferent arteriole, not a venule, drain the glomerulus?
opts: It carries filtrate to the proximal tubule
It lowers resistance so blood leaves faster
It keeps glomerular capillary pressure high for filtration
It lets glomerular blood mix with venous blood
qs.why: An arteriole on the outflow side holds pressure up in the glomerular capillaries, which drives filtration.

qs.q: Efferent arterioles of juxtamedullary nephrons form which capillaries?
qs.why: Juxtamedullary efferent arterioles form the vasa recta, long hairpin capillaries beside the loops; cortical ones form peritubular capillaries.

qs.q: Movement of a substance from the tubular lumen into the interstitium and capillaries is called what?
qs.why: Reabsorption goes from the lumen into the blood; secretion goes the opposite way, from the blood through the tubule cells into the lumen.

qs.q: At which part of the renal corpuscle does the proximal convoluted tubule begin?
qs.why: At the tubular pole the capsular space drains into the PCT; the arterioles enter and leave at the vascular pole.

qs.q: What epithelium forms the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule?
qs.why: The parietal layer is simple squamous and turns into the simple cuboidal epithelium of the PCT at the tubular pole.

qs.q: Which layer of the filtration barrier stops blood cells and platelets?
qs.why: Endothelial pores hold back cells and platelets; the GBM stops large proteins and the slit diaphragms stop many small proteins.

qs.q: Which component gives the glomerular basement membrane its negative charge?
qs.why: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans are strongly anionic and repel negatively charged proteins; type IV collagen forms the size-blocking mesh.

qs.q: What are pedicels?
qs.why: Podocyte primary processes branch into interdigitating pedicels; the gaps between them are the filtration slits.

qs.q: Nephrin is a key protein of which structure?
qs.why: Nephrin molecules from facing pedicels meet across the filtration slit like a zipper, forming the slit diaphragm.

qs.q: What happens when functional nephrin is missing?
opts: Red blood cells pass into the urine
qs.why: Without nephrin the slit diaphragm fails, so protein crosses the filter (congenital nephrotic syndrome).

qs.q: Going from capillary lumen to urinary space, what is the order of the filtration barrier?
qs.why: Fenestrated endothelium lines the capillary, the thick GBM sits in the middle, and pedicels with slit diaphragms face the urinary space.

qs.q: Albumin is near the filter's size cut-off. What mainly keeps it out of the filtrate?
opts: Podocytes take it up by endocytosis
Mesangial cells bind it in the matrix
It is too large for the endothelial pores
Its negative charge is repelled by the barrier
qs.why: Albumin (about 67 kDa) is negatively charged and so is the barrier; charge repulsion keeps it out.

qs.q: Which of these passes freely into the glomerular filtrate?
qs.why: Water, ions, glucose, amino acids and urea are filtered; cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

qs.q: Where in the glomerulus do mesangial cells sit?
opts: In the wall of the afferent arteriole
Between capillary loops, where podocytes do not cover them
Lining the outer wall of Bowman's capsule
qs.why: Mesangial cells and their matrix fill the stalk between capillaries, covering surfaces that lack podocytes.

qs.q: Which is a function of mesangial cells?
opts: Phagocytosing protein aggregates trapped in the filter
qs.why: Mesangial cells support capillaries, contract with pressure changes, clear protein aggregates and secrete cytokines and prostaglandins.

qs.q: Which feature identifies a medullary ray in the renal cortex?
opts: Parallel straight tubules with no corpuscles
qs.why: Medullary rays are bands of straight tubules (proximal straight tubules, thick ascending limbs, collecting ducts); corpuscles sit in the cortical labyrinth.

qs.q: In an H&E glomerulus, nuclei on the outer surface of capillary loops, bulging into the urinary space, belong to which cells?
qs.why: Podocytes sit on the urinary-space side of the capillaries; endothelial nuclei line the lumens and parietal nuclei line the capsule wall.

qs.q: In an H&E glomerulus, darker nuclei in the stalks where capillary loops meet belong to which cells?
qs.why: Mesangial cells sit centrally between loops and often stain darker than podocytes.

qs.q: Which feature best distinguishes the PCT from the DCT in H&E?
opts: A fuzzy lumen filled by a brush border
qs.why: The PCT has long microvilli (brush border) that make its lumen look filled; the other three options describe the DCT.

qs.q: A small cortical tubule has pale cells, crowded nuclei and a clean, open lumen. What is it most likely?
qs.why: DCT cells are smaller and paler with no brush border, so more nuclei show per section and the lumen looks empty.

qs.q: Why is PCT cytoplasm deeply eosinophilic?
qs.why: Many long mitochondria, packed in the basal folds to power Na⁺ pumps, stain the cytoplasm deep pink.

qs.q: What do the apical vesicles and lysosomes of PCT cells do?
opts: Digest reabsorbed small proteins into amino acids
qs.why: Filtered small proteins are taken up in apical vesicles and broken down in lysosomes; the amino acids go back to the blood.

qs.q: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells are modified versions of which cells?
opts: Smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole
Endothelial cells of the efferent arteriole
Epithelial cells of the distal tubule
qs.why: JG cells are smooth muscle cells in the afferent arteriole's wall that became secretory and release renin.

qs.q: How is the macula densa recognized in a section?
opts: Tall distal-tubule cells with crowded nuclei
Granular cells in an arteriole wall
Cells with a dense brush border
qs.why: Where the distal tubule touches its own corpuscle, its cells become tall and tightly packed, so their nuclei look crowded.

qs.q: When NaCl reaching the macula densa rises, what happens?
opts: Mesangial cells relax and GFR rises
The efferent arteriole dilates and GFR rises
The afferent arteriole constricts and GFR falls
qs.why: High NaCl signals a high GFR, so the macula densa makes the afferent arteriole constrict, bringing GFR back down.

qs.q: How does aldosterone raise blood volume?
opts: It converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
It inserts aquaporins in the PCT
It increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the DCT and collecting ducts
qs.why: More Na⁺ is reabsorbed and water follows it; vasoconstriction is angiotensin II's direct effect.

qs.q: Which feature identifies a medullary collecting duct?
opts: Pale cells with sharp cell borders
A wall of flat squamous cells
A brush border filling the lumen
Deep pink cells with crowded nuclei
qs.why: Collecting ducts are the largest medullary tubules, lined by pale cuboidal-to-columnar principal cells with distinct borders.

qs.q: In the medulla, which feature marks a vasa recta capillary rather than a thin limb?
opts: Red blood cells in the lumen
qs.why: Both are thin-walled tubes, but the capillary usually holds red blood cells and has an even thinner wall.

qs.q: How does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
opts: It opens Na⁺ channels in intercalated cells
It adds microvilli to the duct cells
It inserts aquaporins into principal cells' luminal membrane
qs.why: ADH moves stored aquaporin vesicles into the luminal membrane, so water leaves the duct toward the salty medulla.

qs.q: Which feature distinguishes transitional epithelium from stratified squamous epithelium?
opts: Large dome-shaped umbrella cells on the surface
qs.why: Urothelium's surface cells are big, dome-shaped and sometimes binucleate; stratified squamous surface cells are flat.

qs.q: Which structure is lined by transitional epithelium?
qs.why: Calyces, renal pelvis, ureters and bladder all have transitional epithelium; the distal urethra is stratified squamous.

qs.q: What do uroplakin plaques on umbrella cells do?
opts: Shield the cells from hypertonic urine
Pump Na⁺ out of the urine
qs.why: Uroplakins stiffen the apical membrane into plaques that, with tight junctions, form an osmotic barrier against hypertonic urine.

qs.q: Which feature identifies the ureter in cross-section?
opts: Thin walls with a brush-border lining
A star-shaped lumen and a thick smooth-muscle layer
A wide lumen with stratified squamous lining
A lumen lined by simple cuboidal cells
qs.why: Longitudinal mucosal folds make a star-shaped lumen lined by urothelium, and the muscle layer is much thicker than the mucosa.

qs.q: How does the urothelium look when the bladder is full?
qs.why: Filling stretches the mucosa smooth and thins the urothelium (5–7 layers empty vs 2–3 full); umbrella cells flatten.

qs.q: What epithelium lines the distal end of the urethra, at its outside opening?
qs.why: The urethra is mostly stratified or pseudostratified columnar but ends as stratified squamous epithelium at the opening.
